\section*{A Reliable Translation Process}
\lessonobjective{Turn a verbal situation into variables, equations, derivatives, and a contextual conclusion.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
The model in \emph{How to Translate Derivative Word Problems} is a simplified mathematical description, not reality itself. Begin by identifying inputs, outputs, units, assumptions, and the range over which the formula is intended to be credible. The derivative then measures sensitivity inside that model.

Interpret both the amount and its rate. A peak may occur where the derivative is zero, but a decision based on that peak must still respect constraints and model limitations. Strong applied work includes a reasonableness check and says what the calculation does not establish.
\end{bgexposition}

\BGVTwoBTranslatePipeline



\begin{bgexposition}[title={A word problem is a model-building problem before it is a calculus problem}]
The derivative is rarely the first line of work. Begin by naming the quantities, assigning units, and deciding which variable depends on which. Draw a diagram when geometry is involved. Write one equation that expresses the relationship, and only then differentiate.

The final sentence matters as much as the derivative. It should identify the quantity changing, the input with respect to which it changes, the instant or state being considered, the sign, and the units. This translation is what turns a correct calculation into an answer to the actual question.
\end{bgexposition}

A word problem is not a decorative version of a formula exercise. It asks you to build the mathematical object before using it. That is why students can know every derivative rule and still feel stuck when a ladder slides, a balloon rises, or a company changes production.

Use the following translation process.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Name the variables.} Include units and identify which variable depends on which.
\item \textbf{Write what is known.} Separate constant values from rates such as \(dx/dt\).
\item \textbf{Build one governing relationship.} Use geometry, a physical law, or a stated model.
\item \textbf{Differentiate before inserting the changing snapshot.} The relationship must remain valid while the quantities change.
\item \textbf{Substitute the instant-specific values.}
\item \textbf{Solve for the requested rate or quantity.}
\item \textbf{Interpret the sign, units, and size.}
\end{enumerate}

\begin{bgguided}[title={The whole application loop in a simple setting}]
The radius of a circular spill grows at \(0.3\) meters per minute. How fast is its area growing when the radius is \(5\) meters?
\begin{bgsolution}
Name the variables:
\[
r=r(t)\text{ meters},\qquad A=A(t)\text{ square meters}.
\]
Known rate:
\[
\frac{dr}{dt}=0.3\text{ m/min}.
\]
Relationship:
\[
A=\pi r^2.
\]
Differentiate with respect to time:
\[
\frac{dA}{dt}=2\pi r\frac{dr}{dt}.
\]
Now insert the snapshot \(r=5\):
\[
\frac{dA}{dt}=2\pi(5)(0.3)=3\pi.
\]
Therefore the spill area is increasing at
\[
\boxed{3\pi\text{ m}^2/\text{min}}
\]
when the radius is \(5\) meters.
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgmistake}[title={A number without a sentence is unfinished}]
The value \(3\pi\) alone does not identify what is changing, in which direction, or in what units. In an application, the interpretation is part of the answer rather than optional decoration added after the mathematics has already left the building.
\end{bgmistake}

\chapter{Interpreting Higher Derivatives, Motion, and Change}
\section{From Computation to Interpretation}
\lessonobjective{Compute and interpret second and higher derivatives.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
The graphs in \emph{Higher Derivatives} should be read vertically through a common input. A height on the derivative graph is a slope on the original graph. A zero of velocity is a horizontal tangent of position; a zero of acceleration is a horizontal tangent of velocity.

Do not match graphs by superficial shape. Translate one feature at a time: sign, zeros, increasing behavior, and concavity. This produces a defensible interpretation even when the graphs are unfamiliar or not drawn to a convenient scale.
\end{bgexposition}




\begin{bgexposition}[title={Rates have their own rates}]
A positive first derivative means an amount is increasing; it does not tell you whether that increase is speeding up or slowing down. The second derivative answers that second question by measuring change in the first derivative.

Keep the levels separate. In motion, position can be decreasing while acceleration is positive. In economics, cost can be rising while marginal cost is falling. The signs refer to different layers of behavior.
\end{bgexposition}

A derivative is itself a function, so it can be differentiated again. The second derivative measures how the first derivative changes, the third measures how the second changes, and so on. These layers encode acceleration, changing curvature, changing growth rates, and the shape of local approximations.

Higher derivatives are meaningful only when the required differentiability exists. A function may have a first derivative without having a second, so the notation \(f^{(n)}\) quietly carries a regularity assumption.

The derivative \(f'\) is itself a function, so it may have a derivative. The second derivative is
\[
f''(x)=\frac{d}{dx}f'(x)=\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}.
\]
Higher derivatives are written
\[
f^{(3)}(x),\quad f^{(4)}(x),\quad \ldots,\quad f^{(n)}(x).
\]

The first derivative measures how \(f\) changes. The second derivative measures how the first derivative changes. Its units are output units per input unit per input unit.

\begin{bgguided}[title={Compute several derivative levels}]
Let
\[
f(x)=x^4-3x^3+2x.
\]
Find \(f'\), \(f''\), \(f^{(3)}\), and \(f^{(4)}\).
\begin{bgsolution}
Differentiate repeatedly:
\[
f'(x)=4x^3-9x^2+2,
\]
\[
f''(x)=12x^2-18x,
\]
\[
f^{(3)}(x)=24x-18,
\]
\[
\boxed{f^{(4)}(x)=24}.
\]
A fifth derivative would be zero.
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgconcept}[title={Second derivative as changing slope}]
If \(f''(a)>0\), then slopes of \(f\) are increasing near \(a\). If \(f''(a)<0\), slopes are decreasing. This is the foundation of concavity, developed later.
\end{bgconcept}


\begin{bgapplication}[title={Jerk and elevator comfort}]
If an elevator's position is \(s(t)\), then \(s'\) is velocity, \(s''\) acceleration, and \(s^{(3)}\) jerk. Passengers notice abrupt changes in acceleration even when the acceleration itself remains within safe limits. Motion-control systems therefore smooth jerk as well as speed and acceleration. Higher derivatives can measure physically distinct layers of change.
\end{bgapplication}

\begin{bgadvanced}[title={Smooth does not always mean analytic}]
A function may possess derivatives of every order and still fail to equal its Taylor series. The classic example
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}e^{-1/x^2},&x\ne0,\\0,&x=0\end{cases}
\]
has every derivative equal to zero at the origin, so its Taylor series there is identically zero, while the function is positive away from zero. Later analysis distinguishes infinitely differentiable functions from analytic functions.
\end{bgadvanced}

\section{One-Dimensional Motion}
\lessonobjective{Translate among position, velocity, acceleration, and speed.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
Applied derivative values in \emph{Position, Velocity, and Acceleration} need interpretation, not just calculation. The number, sign, units, and scale all matter. A derivative of $4$ could mean four dollars per item, four meters per second, or four degrees per meter; those are completely different claims.

When data rather than a formula are given, state that the derivative is estimated. Identify the finite difference used, preserve the units, and report precision consistent with the measurements. More decimal places do not create more information.
\end{bgexposition}

\BGVTwoBMotionStack




\begin{bgexposition}[title={Motion uses three related graphs, not one interchangeable picture}]
Position tells where the object is, velocity tells how position is changing, and acceleration tells how velocity is changing. A positive position does not imply positive velocity, and a negative velocity does not imply negative acceleration.

When reading a motion problem, ask one question at a time: where is the object, which direction is it moving, how fast is it moving, and is its velocity becoming more positive or more negative? The derivative relationships connect the answers without collapsing them into one number.
\end{bgexposition}

In one-dimensional motion, position tells where an object is, velocity tells how position changes, and acceleration tells how velocity changes. These are related functions, not interchangeable labels. In particular, velocity can be zero while acceleration is not, as at the top of a vertical toss.

Signs describe direction relative to the chosen coordinate axis. A negative velocity is not ``bad'' and a positive acceleration does not necessarily mean speeding up. Interpretation requires comparing both signs.

If \(s(t)\) is position, then
\[
\boxed{v(t)=s'(t)},
\qquad
\boxed{a(t)=v'(t)=s''(t)}.
\]
Velocity is signed. Positive velocity means motion in the positive direction; negative velocity means motion in the negative direction. Speed is
\[
\boxed{|v(t)|}.
\]
A particle is at rest when \(v(t)=0\). It changes direction only if velocity changes sign, not merely because velocity is zero at one instant.

\begin{bgguided}[title={Complete motion analysis from a position formula}]
A particle has position
\[
s(t)=t^3-6t^2+9t,
\qquad 0\le t\le5.
\]
Find velocity, acceleration, rest times, and intervals of forward and backward motion.
\begin{bgsolution}
Differentiate position:
\[
v(t)=3t^2-12t+9=3(t-1)(t-3).
\]
Differentiate velocity:
\[
a(t)=6t-12.
\]
The particle is at rest when
\[
3(t-1)(t-3)=0,
\]
so \(t=1\) and \(t=3\).

Use a sign chart for velocity:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{c|ccc}
interval&\((0,1)\)&\((1,3)\)&\((3,5)\)\\\hline
sign of \(v\)&+&-&+
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Therefore the particle moves forward on \((0,1)\cup(3,5)\) and backward on \((1,3)\). Velocity changes sign at both rest times, so the particle changes direction at \(t=1\) and \(t=3\).
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgmistake}
Speeding up is not the same as positive acceleration. An object speeds up when velocity and acceleration have the same sign, because the magnitude \(|v|\) is increasing. It slows down when their signs differ.
\end{bgmistake}


\begin{bgmodelinglab}[title={A delivery drone's vertical motion}]
Suppose height is
\[
s(t)=2t^3-15t^2+24t+5
\]
meters. Then
\[
v(t)=6t^2-30t+24,
\qquad
a(t)=12t-30.
\]
At \(t=1\), \(v=0\) and \(a=-18\), so the drone is instantaneously at rest but about to move downward. Solving \(v(t)=0\) identifies all turning times; evaluating \(s\) there reveals the corresponding heights.
\end{bgmodelinglab}

\section{Contextual Derivatives from Data}
\lessonobjective{Estimate and interpret first and second derivatives in applied tables.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
In \emph{Rates from Data and Units}, separate the amount from its rate and the rate from its rate of change. Position, velocity, and acceleration may be evaluated at the same time, but they answer different questions and carry different units. A negative value describes direction or signed change; it does not automatically mean the quantity is small or slowing.

When reading a context, write a sentence for each derivative before calculating. Include what changes, with respect to what, at which input, and in what units. Then use signs to describe direction and compare signs of velocity and acceleration to determine whether speed is increasing or decreasing.
\end{bgexposition}

\BGVTwoBDataRates




\begin{bgexposition}[title={Data give approximations whose quality depends on spacing and noise}]
A table cannot directly display an instantaneous rate because its rows are separated by finite intervals. Forward, backward, and central differences estimate the derivative by nearby secant slopes. Central differences are often more balanced because they use information on both sides.

Smaller spacing is not automatically better when measurements are noisy. Differentiation magnifies small fluctuations, so a responsible estimate reports the data interval and treats the result as approximate.
\end{bgexposition}

A table records finite differences, not exact instantaneous rates. Central differences often improve an estimate by using data on both sides of the target point, but every estimate inherits measurement error and spacing limitations from the data.

Context determines whether the number is plausible. A derivative of temperature with respect to time has different units and meaning from a derivative of temperature with respect to depth. Writing the units forces you to identify which relationship the data actually describes.

Suppose \(T(t)\) is temperature. Then \(T'\) measures temperature change per unit time. The second derivative \(T''\) measures how the warming or cooling rate itself changes.

\begin{bgguided}[title={First and second derivative estimates}]
A substance has temperatures
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
t&0&5&10&15&20\\\hline
T(t)&20&31&39&45&49
\end{array}
\]
where \(t\) is minutes and \(T\) is Celsius. Estimate \(T'(10)\) and \(T''(10)\).
\begin{bgsolution}
Use a central difference for the first derivative:
\[
T'(10)\approx\frac{T(15)-T(5)}{10}=\frac{45-31}{10}=1.4\ ^\circ\mathrm C/\mathrm{min}.
\]
Estimate nearby derivative values:
\[
T'(5)\approx\frac{T(10)-T(0)}{10}=1.9,
\]
\[
T'(15)\approx\frac{T(20)-T(10)}{10}=1.0.
\]
Then
\[
T''(10)\approx\frac{1.0-1.9}{10}=-0.09\ ^\circ\mathrm C/\mathrm{min}/\mathrm{min}.
\]
The substance is warming, but the warming rate is decreasing.
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgmistake}
A negative second derivative does not mean the original quantity is decreasing. It means the first derivative is decreasing. Temperature can rise while its warming rate falls.
\end{bgmistake}


\begin{bgapplication}[title={Groundwater temperature gradient}]
If temperature readings are taken at depths \(95\), \(100\), and \(105\) meters, then a central estimate
\[
T'(100)\approx\frac{T(105)-T(95)}{10}
\]
has units degrees Celsius per meter. This is a spatial derivative, not a heating rate in time. Such gradients help describe geological heat flow and illustrate why the independent variable belongs in every interpretation.
\end{bgapplication}

\chapter{Linear Approximation, Differentials, and Newton's Method}
\section{A Smooth Curve Looks Like Its Tangent Up Close}
\lessonobjective{Explain local linearity and construct a linearization.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
The approximation in \emph{Local Linearity} replaces a nonlinear function with its best local line. The known value supplies the starting height, and the derivative supplies the rate of change. The estimate is useful because lines are easy to calculate with, not because the original curve has become exactly linear.

Always identify the center $a$ and the target $x$. Write $\Delta x=x-a$, calculate the predicted change $f'(a)\Delta x$, and then add it to $f(a)$. Use concavity or a numerical comparison to understand the direction and size of the error.
\end{bgexposition}




\begin{bgexposition}[title={A differentiable curve has a best local line}]
The tangent line is not merely a line that touches the graph. Near the contact point, it reproduces the function's value and first-order change. As you zoom in, the remaining difference between curve and line becomes small compared with the horizontal displacement.

This is why derivatives support approximation. Instead of evaluating a difficult function exactly at a nearby input, evaluate the tangent line, whose arithmetic is simple. The approximation is local, so distance from the base point matters.
\end{bgexposition}

A differentiable curve resembles a line when viewed closely enough. This is not merely a visual curiosity; it is the operational meaning of differentiability. The tangent line captures the function's first-order response to a small input change.

Local linearity explains why derivatives are useful even when exact formulas are complicated. Near a known input, the function can be replaced temporarily by a much simpler line, with an error that becomes relatively smaller as the input change shrinks.

Differentiability means more than possessing a tangent slope. Near a differentiable point, the function is well approximated by its tangent line. If \(x\) is close to \(a\), then
\[
f(x)\approx f(a)+f'(a)(x-a).
\]

\begin{bgdefinition}[title={Linearization}]
The linearization of \(f\) at \(x=a\) is
\[
\boxed{L(x)=f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)}.
\]
It is exactly the tangent-line function at \(a\).
\end{bgdefinition}

\begin{bgguided}[title={Approximate a square root}]
Use linearization to estimate \(\sqrt{4.1}\).
\begin{bgsolution}
Choose a nearby easy input \(a=4\) for \(f(x)=\sqrt x\). Then
\[
f(4)=2,
\qquad
f'(x)=\frac1{2\sqrt x},
\qquad
f'(4)=\frac14.
\]
The linearization is
\[
L(x)=2+\frac14(x-4).
\]
At \(x=4.1\),
\[
L(4.1)=2+\frac14(0.1)=2.025.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\sqrt{4.1}\approx2.025}.
\]
The true value is about \(2.02485\), so the tangent estimate is close.
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}
\begin{axis}[width=.82\textwidth,height=.42\textwidth,xmin=2.5,xmax=5.5,ymin=1.4,ymax=2.5,axis lines=middle,grid=both,major grid style={draw=BGLine},minor grid style={draw=BGLine!35},minor tick num=1,xlabel={$x$},ylabel={$y$}]
\addplot[BGInk,very thick,domain=2.5:5.5,samples=100]{sqrt(x)};
\addplot[BGGreen,very thick,domain=2.5:5.5]{2+.25*(x-4)};
\addplot[only marks,mark=*,BGGold] coordinates {(4,2)};
\node[anchor=north west,font=\small] at (axis cs:4.05,2) {contact point};
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
\caption{Near \(x=4\), the graph of \(\sqrt x\) is nearly indistinguishable from its tangent line.}
\end{figure}

\begin{bggraphspec}
Function \(f(x)=\sqrt x\); tangent at \(a=4\); windows should include a wide view \(0\le x\le9\) and a linked zoom \(3.7\le x\le4.3\). Display \(f(x)-L(x)\) numerically as the user moves \(x\).
\end{bggraphspec}
\begin{bgeditorialvisual}[title={Existing visual 2B-E02 - square-root curve and its linearization}]
\textbf{Purpose.} The graph introduces local linearity before the approximation formula becomes routine. The learner should see both that the tangent is not the curve and that the difference becomes difficult to detect near the contact point.

\textbf{Composition.} Plot $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ and $L(x)=2+\frac14(x-4)$, mark $(4,2)$, and preserve a wide view. The web edition should pair this with a linked magnified view whose window is controlled by a zoom slider. Display the signed error $f(x)-L(x)$ and the absolute error.

\textbf{Interaction.} The learner moves a target point, predicts whether the tangent overestimates or underestimates based on concavity, and then reveals the true value. A second slider shrinks $|x-4|$ and shows the error relative to the displacement. Avoid displaying so many decimals that the numerical readout becomes the lesson.

\textbf{Accessibility.} Alt text should name both formulas, the contact point, and the fact that the tangent lies above the concave-down square-root curve near the point. On mobile, stack wide and zoomed views and put the error table below.
\end{bgeditorialvisual}


\begin{bgadvanced}[title={The derivative as the best first-order approximation}]
The rigorous statement of local linearity is
\[
\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)-f'(a)h}{h}=0.
\]
The numerator is the approximation error. Dividing by \(h\) and obtaining zero means the error shrinks faster than the input displacement itself. This is the one-variable prototype of the Frechet derivative used in advanced analysis.
\end{bgadvanced}

\section{Zooming In Turns Smooth Curves into Lines}
\lessonobjective{Explain local linearity before using a linearization formula.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
Newton's method in \emph{Why a Tangent Line Can Approximate a Curve} repeatedly uses local linearity to solve a nonlinear equation. Each tangent line supplies an easier zero, which becomes the next estimate. The method can be spectacularly fast near a suitable root and unreliable from a poor starting point.

Record the iteration formula and a table of estimates. Check the function value as well as the digits of $x_n$. A sequence that appears stable on a calculator display may still have converged to the wrong root, entered a cycle, or encountered a nearly horizontal tangent.
\end{bgexposition}

\BGVTwoBLocalLinearity



\begin{bgexposition}[title={Zooming is a mathematical test, not just a picture trick}]
A smooth graph looks straighter under magnification because its nonlinear error shrinks faster than the input change. The derivative is the slope of the line that survives this zooming process.

The phrase ``nearby'' cannot be removed. A tangent line may be excellent over a small interval and terrible far away. Every linear approximation should name its center and give some reason the target input is close enough.
\end{bgexposition}

A smooth curve is not globally a line, but near one point it becomes difficult to distinguish from its tangent line. Differentiability is exactly the condition that the linear error becomes small compared with the input change.

The approximation
\[
f(a+\Delta x)\approx f(a)+f'(a)\Delta x
\]
does not claim that the curve and tangent are identical. It claims that the tangent captures the first-order change near \(a\). The approximation improves as \(\Delta x\) shrinks, unless numerical or measurement limitations become dominant.

\begin{bgtranslation}[title={The mental model}]
Use a nearby input where the function is easy. Start from the known value, then add ``slope times horizontal change.''
\end{bgtranslation}

\section{Choose a Nearby Base Point}
\lessonobjective{Select useful base points and estimate function values.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
The approximation in \emph{Using Linearization} replaces a nonlinear function with its best local line. The known value supplies the starting height, and the derivative supplies the rate of change. The estimate is useful because lines are easy to calculate with, not because the original curve has become exactly linear.

Always identify the center $a$ and the target $x$. Write $\Delta x=x-a$, calculate the predicted change $f'(a)\Delta x$, and then add it to $f(a)$. Use concavity or a numerical comparison to understand the direction and size of the error.
\end{bgexposition}




\begin{bgexposition}[title={Choose a base point where both the function and derivative are easy}]
Linearization works best when the center \(a\) is close to the target and \(f(a)\) is known exactly. Perfect squares, perfect cubes, familiar angles, and simple exponential values are natural anchors.

Write the line \(L(x)=f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)\) before substituting the target. This keeps the derivative calculation, line construction, and numerical estimate as separate checkable steps.
\end{bgexposition}

A linearization is most effective when the base point is close to the target and the function value and derivative are easy to compute there. The method trades exactness for speed while keeping the approximation anchored to real local behavior.

Do not choose a base point merely because it is an integer. Choose one that makes the function genuinely easy and keeps the displacement small. A nearby perfect square is useful for square roots; a nearby familiar angle is useful for trigonometric functions.

A good base point \(a\) is close to the target and makes both \(f(a)\) and \(f'(a)\) easy.

\begin{bgguided}[title={Estimate a cube root}]
Estimate \(\sqrt[3]{26}\).
\begin{bgsolution}
Let \(f(x)=x^{1/3}\). The nearby perfect cube is \(27\), so use \(a=27\):
\[
f(27)=3,
\qquad
f'(x)=\frac1{3x^{2/3}},
\qquad
f'(27)=\frac1{27}.
\]
Thus
\[
L(x)=3+\frac1{27}(x-27).
\]
At \(x=26\),
\[
\boxed{\sqrt[3]{26}\approx3-\frac1{27}=\frac{80}{27}\approx2.963}.
\]
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexample}[title={Estimate a trigonometric value}]
Near \(a=0\), \(\sin0=0\) and \(\cos0=1\), so
\[
\sin x\approx x.
\]
Thus \(\sin(0.03)\approx0.03\) when the angle is measured in radians.
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgmistake}
A linearization is local. Using the tangent at \(x=4\) to estimate \(\sqrt{100}\) is not a calculus technique; it is an elaborate way to be wrong.
\end{bgmistake}

\begin{bgcheck}{linearization-01}{decimal}{3.025}[Quick check]
Use the tangent to \(\sqrt x\) at \(x=9\) to estimate \(\sqrt{9.15}\).
\begin{bgreveal}
\[
L(x)=3+\frac16(x-9),
\]
so \(L(9.15)=3+0.025=\boxed{3.025}\).
\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}


\begin{bgmodelinglab}[title={Estimate a square root without a calculator}]
Use \(f(x)=\sqrt{x}\) near \(a=100\). Since
\[
f(100)=10,
\qquad f'(100)=\frac1{20},
\]
the linearization is
\[
L(x)=10+\frac{x-100}{20}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\sqrt{102}\approx10+\frac2{20}=10.1.
\]
The actual value is slightly below \(10.1\) because \(\sqrt{x}\) is concave down, so its tangent line lies above the curve.
\end{bgmodelinglab}

\section{Differentials and Small Changes}
\lessonobjective{Use \(dy=f'(x)dx\) to estimate changes in an output.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
The approximation in \emph{Differentials} replaces a nonlinear function with its best local line. The known value supplies the starting height, and the derivative supplies the rate of change. The estimate is useful because lines are easy to calculate with, not because the original curve has become exactly linear.

Always identify the center $a$ and the target $x$. Write $\Delta x=x-a$, calculate the predicted change $f'(a)\Delta x$, and then add it to $f(a)$. Use concavity or a numerical comparison to understand the direction and size of the error.
\end{bgexposition}

\BGVTwoBDifferentials




\begin{bgexposition}[title={Differentials package the tangent-line prediction}]
For an input change \(dx\), the differential \(dy=f'(x)dx\) is the change predicted by the tangent line. The actual change is \(\Delta y=f(x+dx)-f(x)\). Near the base point, \(dy\) and \(\Delta y\) are close but not generally equal.

This notation is especially useful in measurement problems because it keeps the estimated output error attached to the input uncertainty and local sensitivity.
\end{bgexposition}

Differentials package the linear approximation into the compact relation
\[
dy=f'(x)\,dx.
\]
Here \(dx\) represents a chosen small input change, and \(dy\) represents the corresponding linearized output change. The actual change \(\Delta y\) is usually close to, but not exactly equal to, \(dy\).

This notation is especially useful when several measurements contribute to an engineering calculation. It preserves units and makes first-order error propagation visible.

If \(y=f(x)\), define the input differential \(dx\) as a chosen small change in \(x\). The corresponding differential in \(y\) is
\[
\boxed{dy=f'(x)\,dx}.
\]
The actual output change is
\[
\Delta y=f(x+\Delta x)-f(x).
\]
For small \(\Delta x\),
\[
\Delta y\approx dy.
\]

\begin{bgguided}[title={Estimate a change in area}]
A circular plate has radius \(10\) cm. Estimate the change in area if the radius increases by \(0.03\) cm.
\begin{bgsolution}
Area is
\[
A=\pi r^2.
\]
Therefore
\[
dA=2\pi r\,dr.
\]
Use \(r=10\) and \(dr=0.03\):
\[
dA=2\pi(10)(0.03)=0.6\pi.
\]
Thus the area increases by approximately
\[
\boxed{0.6\pi\approx1.885\text{ cm}^2}.
\]
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgconcept}[title={Derivative as a local conversion factor}]
The relation \(dy=f'(x)dx\) says that near a chosen input, the derivative converts a small input change into an approximate output change.
\end{bgconcept}


\begin{bgmodelinglab}[title={Volume added by a thin coating}]
A metal sphere of radius \(r=10\) cm receives a coating of thickness \(dr=0.02\) cm. Since
\[
V=\frac43\pi r^3,
\qquad dV=4\pi r^2\,dr,
\]
we estimate
\[
dV=4\pi(10)^2(0.02)=8\pi\text{ cm}^3.
\]
This is the surface area times thickness, exactly the geometric shell interpretation expected for a very thin coating.
\end{bgmodelinglab}

\section{Absolute and Relative Error}
\lessonobjective{Use differentials to estimate propagated measurement error.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
Newton's method in \emph{Error Estimation with Differentials} repeatedly uses local linearity to solve a nonlinear equation. Each tangent line supplies an easier zero, which becomes the next estimate. The method can be spectacularly fast near a suitable root and unreliable from a poor starting point.

Record the iteration formula and a table of estimates. Check the function value as well as the digits of $x_n$. A sequence that appears stable on a calculator display may still have converged to the wrong root, entered a cycle, or encountered a nearly horizontal tangent.
\end{bgexposition}




\begin{bgexposition}[title={Error propagation is derivative interpretation with uncertainty as the input change}]
If a measured quantity has uncertainty \(|dx|\), then \(|dy|\approx|f'(x)|\,|dx|\) estimates the resulting output uncertainty. A large derivative magnifies measurement error; a small derivative dampens it.

Relative error compares uncertainty with the size of the quantity itself. State clearly whether the problem asks for absolute error, relative error, or percentage error, because they answer different practical questions.
\end{bgexposition}

Measurements are never infinitely precise. If a radius, voltage, mass, or time is known only within a tolerance, the derivative estimates how that uncertainty affects a computed output. Large derivative magnitude means the output is locally sensitive to input error.

Absolute error and relative error answer different questions. An error of one cubic centimeter may be negligible for a tank and disastrous for a microfluidic device; relative error compares the error with the size of the quantity being estimated.

If an input measurement has possible error \(|dx|\), the propagated absolute output error is approximately
\[
|dy|=|f'(x)||dx|.
\]
Relative error is
\[
\frac{|dy|}{|y|},
\]
and percentage error is the relative error multiplied by \(100\%\).

\begin{bgguided}[title={Error in the volume of a sphere}]
A sphere's radius is measured as \(8\) cm with possible error \(0.02\) cm. Estimate the maximum error in the computed volume and the relative error.
\begin{bgsolution}
\[
V=\frac43\pi r^3,
\qquad
 dV=4\pi r^2dr.
\]
Using \(r=8\) and \(|dr|=0.02\),
\[
|dV|=4\pi(64)(0.02)=5.12\pi\approx16.08\text{ cm}^3.
\]
The volume is
\[
V=\frac43\pi(512)=\frac{2048}{3}\pi.
\]
Relative error:
\[
\frac{|dV|}{V}
=\frac{5.12\pi}{(2048/3)\pi}
=0.0075.
\]
Thus the percentage error is approximately
\[
\boxed{0.75\%}.
\]
For a power \(r^3\), the relative volume error is roughly three times the relative radius error.
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexercises}
\item Estimate the error in \(A=\pi r^2\) when \(r=5\pm0.01\).
\item A cube side is measured with \(0.2\%\) relative error. Estimate the relative error in volume.
\item Explain why relative error is often more informative than absolute error when comparing quantities of different sizes.
\end{bgexercises}


\begin{bgmodelinglab}[title={Manufacturing tolerance in a cylindrical part}]
A cylinder has fixed height \(h=20\) mm and measured radius \(r=5.00\pm0.02\) mm. With
\[
V=\pi r^2h,
\qquad dV=2\pi rh\,dr,
\]
the estimated volume error is
\[
|dV|\approx2\pi(5)(20)(0.02)=4\pi\text{ mm}^3.
\]
The relative error is approximately
\[
\frac{|dV|}{V}=\frac{2|dr|}{r}=0.008,
\]
or \(0.8\%\). Squaring the radius doubles the relative sensitivity.
\end{bgmodelinglab}

\begin{bgadvanced}[title={Sensitivity and condition numbers}]
The derivative measures absolute sensitivity. A dimensionless relative sensitivity is often written
\[
\kappa(x)=\left|\frac{x f'(x)}{f(x)}\right|.
\]
It estimates the relative output error produced by a relative input error. Numerical analysts call this a condition number. A large \(\kappa\) warns that even accurate input data may produce an unstable output.
\end{bgadvanced}
\webexplore{subjects/math/calculus/derivative-applications/advanced-sensitivity-elasticity}{Sensitivity, elasticity, and condition numbers}

\section{Use Tangent Lines to Find Roots}
\lessonobjective{Derive and execute Newton's method; recognize common failure modes.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
Newton's method in \emph{Newton's Method} repeatedly uses local linearity to solve a nonlinear equation. Each tangent line supplies an easier zero, which becomes the next estimate. The method can be spectacularly fast near a suitable root and unreliable from a poor starting point.

Record the iteration formula and a table of estimates. Check the function value as well as the digits of $x_n$. A sequence that appears stable on a calculator display may still have converged to the wrong root, entered a cycle, or encountered a nearly horizontal tangent.
\end{bgexposition}

\BGVTwoBNewton




\begin{bgexposition}[title={Newton's method repeatedly replaces a curve by its tangent line}]
To solve \(f(x)=0\), start with a guess \(x_n\), draw the tangent line there, and use the tangent's \(x\)-intercept as the next guess. Algebraically this gives \(x_{n+1}=x_n-f(x_n)/f'(x_n)\).

The method can converge astonishingly fast near a well-behaved root, but it is not infallible. A poor starting value, a nearly horizontal tangent, or a complicated graph can send the iterates away from the desired root. A graph and a reasoned initial guess are part of the method, not optional decoration.
\end{bgexposition}

Newton's method turns tangent lines into an iterative root finder. Starting from a guess, move to the \(x\)-intercept of the tangent line, draw a new tangent, and repeat. When the geometry is favorable, the approximations improve with startling speed.

The method is powerful, not magical. A poor starting value, a nearly horizontal tangent, or a function with awkward geometry can send the iteration away from the desired root. Numerical methods require both calculation and supervision.

To solve \(f(x)=0\), start with an estimate \(x_n\). The tangent line at \((x_n,f(x_n))\) crosses the \(x\)-axis at a usually improved estimate \(x_{n+1}\).

The tangent line is
\[
y-f(x_n)=f'(x_n)(x-x_n).
\]
Set \(y=0\) and solve for \(x\):
\[
\boxed{x_{n+1}=x_n-\frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}}.
\]

\begin{bgguided}[title={Approximate \(\sqrt2\)}]
Solve \(x^2-2=0\) using \(x_0=1.5\).
\begin{bgsolution}
Let \(f(x)=x^2-2\), so \(f'(x)=2x\). Newton's formula becomes
\[
x_{n+1}=x_n-\frac{x_n^2-2}{2x_n}
=\frac12\left(x_n+\frac2{x_n}\right).
\]
First step:
\[
x_1=\frac12\left(1.5+\frac2{1.5}\right)=1.416666\ldots
\]
Second step:
\[
x_2\approx\frac12\left(1.4166667+\frac2{1.4166667}\right)
\approx1.4142157.
\]
Third step gives
\[
x_3\approx1.4142136.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{\sqrt2\approx1.4142136}.
\]
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgmistake}[title={Newton's method can fail}]
Failure can occur when \(f'(x_n)=0\), when the tangent jumps far from the desired root, when iterates cycle, or when the initial guess lies in a bad region. A graph and a bracketing argument remain useful. Numerical methods are tools, not divine revelation from a calculator display.
\end{bgmistake}

\begin{bggraphspec}
For \(f(x)=x^2-2\), show the curve, a movable initial estimate, each tangent line, and the sequence of \(x\)-intercepts. Include a table of \(n,x_n,f(x_n)\). The animation should permit step-by-step iteration rather than autoplaying past the reasoning.
\end{bggraphspec}
\begin{bgeditorialvisual}[title={Existing visual specification 2B-E03 - Newton iteration tool}]
\textbf{Purpose.} This specification extends the static Newton visual into a complete numerical laboratory. It should make each tangent construction inspectable and make failure modes available rather than presenting only a perfectly convergent example.

\textbf{Required views.} Show the curve, current point, tangent, next intercept, and complete iteration table. Preserve prior intercepts as a light trail so the sequence is visible. Include a residual column $|f(x_n)|$ and, when a benchmark root is known, an error column.

\textbf{Controls and feedback.} Provide step, undo, reset, and starting-value controls. Never autoplay by default. If $f'(x_n)$ is zero or very small, show a specific warning. Include examples that converge to different roots, diverge, or cycle. A textual explanation must accompany every failure state.

\textbf{Accessibility.} Every graphical step must also appear as an equation and table row. Keyboard operation is mandatory. On mobile, show one tangent step at a time with the table immediately below.
\end{bgeditorialvisual}


\begin{bgmodelinglab}[title={Find a break-even production level}]
Suppose profit is
\[
P(q)=-0.01q^2+18q-5000.
\]
To locate a break-even point, solve \(P(q)=0\) with
\[
q_{n+1}=q_n-\frac{P(q_n)}{P'(q_n)},
\qquad P'(q)=-0.02q+18.
\]
Starting from \(q_0=300\) generates a sequence of improving production estimates. A business interpretation still requires choosing the economically relevant positive root and checking whether the model is credible at that output.
\end{bgmodelinglab}

\begin{bgadvanced}[title={Why Newton's method can become spectacularly fast}]
Near a simple root \(r\) with \(f'(r)\ne0\), Newton's method often has quadratic convergence: once an approximation is sufficiently close, the number of correct digits roughly doubles with each step. This follows because the next error is approximately a constant times the square of the current error. Multiple roots, small derivatives, or poor starting values weaken that behavior.
\end{bgadvanced}

\chapter{Related Rates}
\section{Several Quantities Changing Together}
\lessonobjective{Translate a word problem into a differentiable relation and solve for an unknown rate.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
Related-rates work in \emph{Related Rates Workflow} becomes manageable when geometry and calculus are kept separate. Geometry supplies an equation such as the Pythagorean theorem, a volume formula, or a similar-triangle proportion. Calculus differentiates that equation. The derivative does not invent the geometry for you.

Before solving, predict the sign of the unknown rate from the picture. That prediction is a powerful error check. If a ladder foot moves away from a wall, the top should move down; a positive answer for its height rate should trigger a review.
\end{bgexposition}

\BGVTwoBRelatedWorkflow




\begin{bgexposition}[title={All quantities vary with time even when time is not written in the geometry equation}]
A related-rates equation may look like \(x^2+y^2=L^2\), but the moving quantities are really \(x(t)\) and \(y(t)\). Differentiating with respect to time makes the hidden dependence visible through chain-rule factors such as \(dx/dt\) and \(dy/dt\).

Do not substitute the snapshot values before differentiating. Doing so turns changing quantities into constants and destroys the rates you are trying to relate. Differentiate the general relationship first, then evaluate at the specified instant.
\end{bgexposition}

Related-rates problems describe a snapshot of a system whose variables are all changing with time. The governing equation may contain no visible \(t\), but each changing symbol is really a function of time. Differentiating the relation reveals how the rates constrain one another.

The main difficulty is modeling, not differentiation. Draw the situation, name every changing quantity, distinguish constants from variables, write one relation, and only then differentiate. Substituting numbers too early freezes the very quantities whose rates you need.

In a related-rates problem, several variables depend on time and are connected by an equation. Differentiate the relation with respect to time, then use the known values and rates at the instant of interest.

\begin{bgmethod}[title={Reliable related-rates workflow}]
\begin{enumerate}
\item Draw and label a diagram when geometry is involved.
\item Define every changing quantity as a function of time.
\item Record known rates with signs and units.
\item Write one equation relating the changing quantities.
\item Differentiate the equation with respect to time before substituting numerical values.
\item Substitute the instantaneous values and solve for the requested rate.
\item Check sign, magnitude, and units against the physical situation.
\end{enumerate}
\end{bgmethod}

\begin{bgconcept}[title={Why values are substituted after differentiation}]
If you replace a changing radius by the number \(5\) before differentiating, you have turned it into a constant and erased its rate. Differentiate the variable relationship first; use the instantaneous number only after the derivative relation has been created.
\end{bgconcept}

\begin{bgguided}[title={Expanding circle}]
A circular ripple's radius increases at \(3\) cm/s. How fast is its area increasing when the radius is \(10\) cm?
\begin{bgsolution}
Let \(r(t)\) be radius and \(A(t)\) area. The relation is
\[
A=\pi r^2.
\]
Differentiate with respect to time:
\[
\frac{dA}{dt}=2\pi r\frac{dr}{dt}.
\]
Now substitute
\[
r=10,\qquad \frac{dr}{dt}=3.
\]
Then
\[
\frac{dA}{dt}=2\pi(10)(3)=\boxed{60\pi\text{ cm}^2/\text{s}}.
\]
The result is positive because the area is increasing.
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgcheck}{related-basic-01}{expression}{48pi}[Quick check]
A sphere's radius grows at \(2\) cm/s. How fast is its surface area \(S=4\pi r^2\) changing when \(r=3\)?
\begin{bgreveal}
\[
\frac{dS}{dt}=8\pi r\frac{dr}{dt}=8\pi(3)(2)=\boxed{48\pi}.
\]
The canonical metadata should use \(48\pi\), not the placeholder.
\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}


\begin{bgadvanced}[title={Constraint curves and tangent vectors}]
A related-rates equation such as \(F(x,y)=0\) describes a curve of allowable states. As the system moves, the velocity vector \((x',y')\) must remain tangent to that curve. Differentiating gives
\[
F_xx'+F_yy'=0,
\]
which says the gradient \((F_x,F_y)\) is perpendicular to the motion. This geometric viewpoint generalizes related rates to several variables and constrained dynamics.
\end{bgadvanced}

\section{Distances Connected by a Right Triangle}
\lessonobjective{Solve ladder, separation, and distance problems using the Pythagorean theorem.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
In \emph{Pythagorean Related Rates}, distinguish a quantity from its rate and a distance from a component of that distance. Many errors come from assigning one symbol to two different lengths or from confusing the speed of an object with the speed of a shadow tip or line of sight.

Use a variable table if the diagram is crowded: quantity, meaning, units, known value, known rate. The table makes substitutions deliberate and prevents a snapshot value from being mistaken for a constant throughout the motion.
\end{bgexposition}

\BGVTwoBLadder




\begin{bgexposition}[title={Right triangles connect rates along different directions}]
Whenever two changing perpendicular distances and a connecting distance appear, the Pythagorean theorem is the natural relationship. Differentiating \(x^2+y^2=z^2\) gives \(2x\dot x+2y\dot y=2z\dot z\), which weights each rate by the current geometry.

The snapshot lengths matter because the same horizontal speed can produce different changes in the diagonal depending on the triangle's shape at that moment.
\end{bgexposition}

Right-triangle models appear whenever two perpendicular distances determine a third: ladders, aircraft separation, radar range, and objects moving on perpendicular roads. The Pythagorean theorem supplies the constraint, while signs on the rates record the directions of motion.

A length can be positive while its derivative is negative. For example, the height of a ladder remains positive even as it decreases. Confusing a quantity with its rate is one of the quickest ways to produce a physically impossible answer.

\begin{bgguided}[title={Sliding ladder}]
A \(13\)-foot ladder leans against a wall. The bottom slides away from the wall at \(2\) ft/s. How fast is the top sliding down when the bottom is \(5\) feet from the wall?
\begin{bgsolution}
Let \(x(t)\) be the bottom's distance from the wall and \(y(t)\) the height of the top. The ladder length is constant:
\[
x^2+y^2=13^2.
\]
Differentiate:
\[
2x\frac{dx}{dt}+2y\frac{dy}{dt}=0.
\]
At the instant \(x=5\), find \(y\):
\[
5^2+y^2=169\quad\Rightarrow\quad y=12.
\]
Substitute \(dx/dt=2\):
\[
2(5)(2)+2(12)\frac{dy}{dt}=0.
\]
Thus
\[
20+24\frac{dy}{dt}=0,
\]
\[
\boxed{\frac{dy}{dt}=-\frac56\text{ ft/s}}.
\]
The negative sign says the height is decreasing, so the top moves downward at \(5/6\) ft/s.
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexample}[title={Two vehicles moving on perpendicular roads}]
If one vehicle is \(x\) miles east of an intersection and another is \(y\) miles north, their separation \(z\) satisfies
\[
z^2=x^2+y^2.
\]
Differentiating gives
\[
z\frac{dz}{dt}=x\frac{dx}{dt}+y\frac{dy}{dt}.
\]
Signs of \(dx/dt\) and \(dy/dt\) must reflect whether each vehicle moves toward or away from the intersection.
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgmistake}
The constant hypotenuse in a ladder problem has derivative zero. Writing \(2L\,dL/dt\) is not wrong, but \(dL/dt=0\). More often, students mistakenly insert a nonzero rate for a length the problem says is fixed.
\end{bgmistake}


\begin{bgmodelinglab}[title={Two aircraft tracked from a control station}]
Aircraft A is \(30\) km east of a station and moving east at \(600\) km/h. Aircraft B is \(40\) km north and moving south at \(500\) km/h. Their separation \(z\) satisfies
\[
z^2=x^2+y^2.
\]
At the instant described, \(z=50\), \(x'=600\), and \(y'=-500\). Hence
\[
50z'=30(600)+40(-500)=-2000,
\]
so
\[
z'=-40\text{ km/h}.
\]
Despite both aircraft moving rapidly, their separation is decreasing only at \(40\) km/h because the two directional effects nearly cancel.
\end{bgmodelinglab}

\section{Volumes with Changing Dimensions}
\lessonobjective{Relate volume rates to changing heights or radii, including similar-triangle constraints.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
Related-rates work in \emph{Volume and Filling Problems} becomes manageable when geometry and calculus are kept separate. Geometry supplies an equation such as the Pythagorean theorem, a volume formula, or a similar-triangle proportion. Calculus differentiates that equation. The derivative does not invent the geometry for you.

Before solving, predict the sign of the unknown rate from the picture. That prediction is a powerful error check. If a ladder foot moves away from a wall, the top should move down; a positive answer for its height rate should trigger a review.
\end{bgexposition}

\BGVTwoBConeTank




\begin{bgexposition}[title={Volume rates depend on both shape and current size}]
A formula such as \(V=\pi r^2h\) contains several quantities that may vary. The problem statement determines which are changing and whether a geometric constraint links them. Differentiation must include every changing factor.

Units provide a strong check: a volume rate is measured in cubic units per unit time. If the final expression has only square units or lacks time, a variable or rate has probably been omitted.
\end{bgexposition}

Filling and draining problems combine geometry with rates. In a cylinder, the cross-sectional area is constant, so height changes at a steady rate when volume does. In a cone or pyramid, the cross-section changes with height, so the same inflow produces different height rates at different depths.

Similar triangles are the bridge between changing dimensions. They reduce a two-variable volume formula to one geometric variable before differentiation, turning a messy system into a solvable rate equation.

\begin{bgguided}[title={Water rising in a cylindrical tank}]
Water enters a cylindrical tank of radius \(4\) m at \(6\) m\(^3\)/min. How fast is the water depth increasing?
\begin{bgsolution}
The water volume is
\[
V=\pi r^2h.
\]
The tank radius is fixed, so \(r=4\):
\[
V=16\pi h.
\]
Differentiate:
\[
\frac{dV}{dt}=16\pi\frac{dh}{dt}.
\]
Substitute \(dV/dt=6\):
\[
\boxed{\frac{dh}{dt}=\frac{3}{8\pi}\text{ m/min}}.
\]
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgguided}[title={Water rising in a cone}]
A conical tank is \(12\) m high with top radius \(4\) m. Water enters at \(2\) m\(^3\)/min. Find \(dh/dt\) when the water is \(3\) m deep.
\begin{bgsolution}
Water volume is
\[
V=\frac13\pi r^2h.
\]
Both \(r\) and \(h\) change, but similar triangles relate them:
\[
\frac rh=\frac4{12}=\frac13,
\qquad r=\frac h3.
\]
Substitute into volume before differentiating:
\[
V=\frac13\pi\left(\frac h3\right)^2h
=\frac{\pi}{27}h^3.
\]
Differentiate:
\[
\frac{dV}{dt}=\frac{\pi}{9}h^2\frac{dh}{dt}.
\]
At \(h=3\), \(dV/dt=2\):
\[
2=\frac{\pi}{9}(9)\frac{dh}{dt}=\pi\frac{dh}{dt}.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{\frac{dh}{dt}=\frac2\pi\text{ m/min}}.
\]
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexamnote}
In a cone, the water surface radius is not the tank's fixed top radius until the tank is full. Similar triangles eliminate the extra variable.
\end{bgexamnote}

\section{Shadows and Proportional Geometry}
\lessonobjective{Build and differentiate similar-triangle relations for shadow problems.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
Related-rates work in \emph{Shadows and Similar Triangles} becomes manageable when geometry and calculus are kept separate. Geometry supplies an equation such as the Pythagorean theorem, a volume formula, or a similar-triangle proportion. Calculus differentiates that equation. The derivative does not invent the geometry for you.

Before solving, predict the sign of the unknown rate from the picture. That prediction is a powerful error check. If a ladder foot moves away from a wall, the top should move down; a positive answer for its height rate should trigger a review.
\end{bgexposition}

\BGVTwoBShadow




\begin{bgexposition}[title={Similar triangles convert a moving light picture into an equation}]
Shadow problems contain two triangles that share an angle and therefore have proportional side lengths. The geometry equation should be built from those proportions before any differentiation occurs.

Define carefully whether a variable measures the person's distance from the light, the shadow length, or the distance from the light to the shadow tip. Confusing those distances is the standard source of a correct derivative applied to the wrong model.
\end{bgexposition}

Shadow problems are proportional-geometry problems in motion. Similar triangles relate heights and horizontal distances, but the wording may ask for the shadow length, the tip position, or the rate at which those two separate quantities change.

Label the complete distance from the light to the tip before writing a proportion. Most shadow errors are not calculus errors; they are diagrams that silently changed which segment a symbol represents.

\begin{bgguided}[title={Walking away from a streetlight}]
A \(6\)-foot person walks away from a \(15\)-foot lamp at \(4\) ft/s. How fast does the tip of the shadow move?
\begin{bgsolution}
Let \(x\) be the person's distance from the lamp and \(s\) the shadow length. The tip is \(x+s\) feet from the lamp.

Similar triangles give
\[
\frac{15}{x+s}=\frac6s.
\]
Cross-multiply:
\[
15s=6x+6s,
\]
so
\[
9s=6x,
\qquad s=\frac23x.
\]
Differentiate:
\[
\frac{ds}{dt}=\frac23\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac83\text{ ft/s}.
\]
The tip position is \(x+s\), so
\[
\frac{d}{dt}(x+s)=4+\frac83=\boxed{\frac{20}{3}\text{ ft/s}}.
\]
The question asks for the tip, not merely the shadow length.
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgmistake}
Shadow problems often contain three horizontal distances: lamp to person, person to tip, and lamp to tip. Name them before writing proportions. Otherwise a correct similar-triangle equation is mostly a matter of luck.
\end{bgmistake}

\section{Angular Rates}
\lessonobjective{Differentiate trigonometric relations involving a changing angle.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
In \emph{Changing Angles}, distinguish a quantity from its rate and a distance from a component of that distance. Many errors come from assigning one symbol to two different lengths or from confusing the speed of an object with the speed of a shadow tip or line of sight.

Use a variable table if the diagram is crowded: quantity, meaning, units, known value, known rate. The table makes substitutions deliberate and prevents a snapshot value from being mistaken for a constant throughout the motion.
\end{bgexposition}

\BGVTwoBRadar




\begin{bgexposition}[title={Angular rates come from differentiating a trigonometric relationship}]
When a line of sight rotates, a right triangle usually links the angle to horizontal and vertical distances. Choosing tangent, sine, or cosine depends on which sides are known and changing.

Differentiate the trigonometric equation before inserting the snapshot. The chain rule will produce \(d\theta/dt\), and the current angle or side lengths will determine the numerical conversion between linear motion and angular motion.
\end{bgexposition}

Angular rates connect linear motion to rotation. A camera tracking a car, a radar dish following an aircraft, or an observer watching a rising object all produce a trigonometric relation between distance and angle.

Angles must be measured in radians for derivative formulas. The resulting rate may be fastest when the object is closest even if its linear speed is constant, because a fixed horizontal displacement sweeps out a larger angle nearby.

\begin{bgguided}[title={Tracking a moving object}]
A camera is \(30\) m from a straight road. A car travels along the road at \(20\) m/s. Let \(x\) be the car's signed distance from the closest road point and \(\theta\) the camera angle, so
\[
\tan\theta=\frac{x}{30}.
\]
Find \(d\theta/dt\) when \(x=40\) m.
\begin{bgsolution}
Differentiate with respect to time:
\[
\sec^2\theta\frac{d\theta}{dt}=\frac1{30}\frac{dx}{dt}.
\]
At \(x=40\), the triangle has adjacent side \(30\), opposite side \(40\), hypotenuse \(50\). Therefore
\[
\sec\theta=\frac{50}{30}=\frac53,
\qquad
\sec^2\theta=\frac{25}{9}.
\]
Substitute \(dx/dt=20\):
\[
\frac{25}{9}\frac{d\theta}{dt}=\frac{20}{30}=\frac23.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{\frac{d\theta}{dt}=\frac6{25}\text{ rad/s}}.
\]
Angular rates are measured in radians per unit time.
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexample}[title={Alternative elimination}]
Since \(\sec^2\theta=1+\tan^2\theta=1+x^2/900\), the angle can be eliminated algebraically before substituting. Both approaches are valid; choose the one that keeps the geometry clearest.
\end{bgexample}


\begin{bgmodelinglab}[title={Radar tracking a climbing aircraft}]
A radar station is \(5\) km from the point directly below an aircraft. If the altitude \(h\) increases at \(0.4\) km/min and
\[
\tan\theta=\frac{h}{5},
\]
then
\[
\sec^2\theta\,\theta'=\frac{h'}5.
\]
At \(h=5\), \(\tan\theta=1\) and \(\sec^2\theta=2\), so
\[
\theta'=\frac{0.4}{10}=0.04\text{ rad/min}.
\]
The angular rate decreases as the aircraft becomes much higher because equal altitude gains subtend smaller additional angles.
\end{bgmodelinglab}

\section{Problems with More Than One Changing Dimension}
\lessonobjective{Handle models where multiple dimensions have independent rates.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
Related-rates work in \emph{Mixed Related-Rates Problems} becomes manageable when geometry and calculus are kept separate. Geometry supplies an equation such as the Pythagorean theorem, a volume formula, or a similar-triangle proportion. Calculus differentiates that equation. The derivative does not invent the geometry for you.

Before solving, predict the sign of the unknown rate from the picture. That prediction is a powerful error check. If a ladder foot moves away from a wall, the top should move down; a positive answer for its height rate should trigger a review.
\end{bgexposition}




\begin{bgexposition}[title={Mixed problems still use the same five-step skeleton}]
Name variables, draw the relationship, differentiate with respect to time, insert the instant, and solve for the requested rate. The surface story may involve water, aircraft, cameras, or expanding objects, but the mathematical skeleton remains stable.

After solving, interpret the sign. A negative rate is often meaningful rather than wrong: a height may be falling, a distance shrinking, or an angle closing.
\end{bgexposition}

Some systems contain several independently changing dimensions. The product rule naturally appears in changing areas, masses, densities, and energies because more than one factor contributes to the total rate.

A negative term does not automatically make the final rate negative. Competing effects can reinforce or cancel. The arithmetic at the end should be interpreted as a balance of mechanisms, not merely a number produced by a formula.

\begin{bgguided}[title={A rectangle changing in both directions}]
A rectangle's length increases at \(3\) cm/s while its width decreases at \(2\) cm/s. How fast is area changing when length is \(10\) cm and width is \(7\) cm?
\begin{bgsolution}
Area is
\[
A=LW.
\]
Differentiate with the product rule:
\[
\frac{dA}{dt}=L\frac{dW}{dt}+W\frac{dL}{dt}.
\]
Use signs:
\[
\frac{dL}{dt}=3,
\qquad
\frac{dW}{dt}=-2.
\]
At \(L=10\), \(W=7\):
\[
\frac{dA}{dt}=10(-2)+7(3)=-20+21=\boxed{1\text{ cm}^2/\text{s}}.
\]
The area is increasing only slightly because the two effects nearly cancel.
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexample}[title={A balloon with changing radius and density}]
If mass \(M=\rho V\), then
\[
\frac{dM}{dt}=\rho\frac{dV}{dt}+V\frac{d\rho}{dt}.
\]
The product rule is itself a related-rates relation whenever both factors depend on time.
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgexercises}
\item A sphere's radius shrinks at \(0.4\) cm/min. Find \(dV/dt\) at \(r=5\).
\item Two cars leave an intersection on perpendicular roads at \(30\) and \(40\) mph. How fast does separation increase after one hour?
\item A \(10\)-foot ladder slides with bottom rate \(1.5\) ft/s. Find the top rate when \(x=6\).
\item Water fills an inverted cone with height \(9\) and radius \(3\) at \(5\) cubic units/min. Find \(dh/dt\) at \(h=6\).
\item A person walks toward a building while the viewing angle to its roof changes. Create a complete variable diagram and rate equation.
\end{bgexercises}


\begin{bgmodelinglab}[title={Gas mass in a changing chamber}]
A chamber contains gas with mass \(M(t)=\rho(t)V(t)\). At one instant, \(\rho=1.2\) kg/m\(^3\), \(V=10\) m\(^3\), \(\rho'=-0.03\) kg/m\(^3\)/min, and \(V'=0.5\) m\(^3\)/min. Then
\[
M'=\rho'V+\rho V'=(-0.03)(10)+(1.2)(0.5)=0.3\text{ kg/min}.
\]
Expansion lowers density, but the increasing volume contributes more strongly, so total mass is rising in this model.
\end{bgmodelinglab}

\chapter{Derivative Theorems and the Shape of a Graph}
\section{Local and Absolute Extrema}
\lessonobjective{Distinguish local and absolute extrema; locate critical numbers and endpoints that may contain extrema.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
The theorem in \emph{Extrema and Critical Numbers} connects global information on an interval with local derivative behavior inside it. Read the hypotheses and conclusion separately. The theorem guarantees existence of at least one point; it may not identify the point, make it unique, or place it at the midpoint.

Use a diagram to understand the claim, then return to algebra to find candidate values when the problem asks for them. A correct theorem citation should name the interval and explain why each hypothesis is satisfied.
\end{bgexposition}

\BGVTwoBExtrema




\begin{bgexposition}[title={An extreme value can occur where the derivative is zero, undefined, or at an endpoint}]
A horizontal tangent is one possible signal of a local maximum or minimum, but it is not a guarantee. Flat points can also occur where the function continues through without turning. Critical numbers identify candidates that require further analysis.

Endpoints belong to absolute-extreme problems even though the ordinary two-sided derivative is not available there. Keeping local and absolute questions separate prevents missing the true largest or smallest value on a closed interval.
\end{bgexposition}

Optimization begins with vocabulary. A local maximum beats nearby values; an absolute maximum beats every feasible value. Critical numbers are inputs where \(f'=0\) or \(f'\) fails to exist, but they are candidates, not automatic extrema.

A function can pass through a critical number without turning, as \(x^3\) does at the origin. The derivative identifies places worth investigating; additional sign or value analysis decides what actually happens.

A local maximum is larger than nearby function values. A local minimum is smaller than nearby values. An absolute maximum or minimum is largest or smallest on the entire domain or interval under consideration.

\begin{bgdefinition}[title={Critical number}]
A number \(c\) in the domain of \(f\) is critical when
\[
f'(c)=0
\]
or \(f'(c)\) does not exist.
\end{bgdefinition}

Critical numbers are candidates, not automatic extrema. Endpoints are also candidates for absolute extrema on closed intervals.

\begin{bgtheorem}[title={Fermat's theorem}]
If \(f\) has a local extremum at an interior point \(c\) and \(f'(c)\) exists, then
\[
f'(c)=0.
\]
\end{bgtheorem}

\begin{bgguided}[title={Find critical numbers}]
Find the critical numbers of
\[
f(x)=x^3-3x^2-9x+1.
\]
\begin{bgsolution}
Differentiate:
\[
f'(x)=3x^2-6x-9=3(x-3)(x+1).
\]
The derivative exists for all \(x\). Set it equal to zero:
\[
3(x-3)(x+1)=0.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{x=-1,\ 3}
\]
are the critical numbers.
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexample}[title={A critical number where the derivative fails}]
For \(f(x)=|x|\), \(x=0\) is critical because \(f'(0)\) does not exist. It is also a local and absolute minimum. A search only for \(f'=0\) would miss it.
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgcheck}{critical-01}{set}{-2,0,2}[Quick check]
Find the critical numbers of \(f(x)=x^4-8x^2\).
\begin{bgreveal}
\[
f'(x)=4x^3-16x=4x(x-2)(x+2),
\]
so \(\boxed{-2,0,2}\).
\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}

pages.source_latex:
\section{Equal Endpoints Force a Horizontal Tangent}
\lessonobjective{Verify hypotheses and apply Rolle's Theorem.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
The theorem in \emph{Rolle's Theorem} connects global information on an interval with local derivative behavior inside it. Read the hypotheses and conclusion separately. The theorem guarantees existence of at least one point; it may not identify the point, make it unique, or place it at the midpoint.

Use a diagram to understand the claim, then return to algebra to find candidate values when the problem asks for them. A correct theorem citation should name the interval and explain why each hypothesis is satisfied.
\end{bgexposition}




\begin{bgexposition}[title={Equal endpoint heights force at least one horizontal tangent}]
Rolle's Theorem describes a smooth trip that begins and ends at the same height. Somewhere between, the function must stop rising and begin falling, stop falling and begin rising, or remain level; in every case a horizontal tangent occurs.

The hypotheses matter. A jump, corner, or missing endpoint can defeat the conclusion. Checking continuity and differentiability is part of applying the theorem, not bureaucratic decoration.
\end{bgexposition}

Rolle's Theorem formalizes a geometric inevitability: if a smooth curve begins and ends at the same height, then somewhere between those endpoints it must have a horizontal tangent. The theorem does not locate the point; it guarantees one exists.

Every hypothesis has a job. Continuity prevents a jump over the conclusion, differentiability prevents a sharp turn, and equal endpoint values create the horizontal average slope that the derivative must match.

\begin{bgtheorem}[title={Rolle's Theorem}]
If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), differentiable on \((a,b)\), and
\[
f(a)=f(b),
\]
then there exists at least one \(c\in(a,b)\) such that
\[
\boxed{f'(c)=0}.
\]
\end{bgtheorem}

\begin{bgconcept}
A smooth trip that begins and ends at the same height must have at least one interior moment with horizontal tangent. The theorem guarantees existence; it does not say the point is unique.
\end{bgconcept}

\begin{bgguided}[title={Find Rolle points}]
Verify Rolle's Theorem for
\[
f(x)=x^2-4x+3
\]
on \([1,3]\), and find \(c\).
\begin{bgsolution}
The function is a polynomial, so it is continuous and differentiable. Endpoint values are
\[
f(1)=0,
\qquad
f(3)=0.
\]
Thus the hypotheses hold. Differentiate:
\[
f'(x)=2x-4.
\]
Set \(f'(c)=0\):
\[
2c-4=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad\boxed{c=2}.
\]
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgmistake}
A theorem conclusion cannot be used until its hypotheses are checked. A function with a corner or discontinuity may have equal endpoint values but fail the differentiability or continuity requirement.
\end{bgmistake}

\section{An Instantaneous Rate Must Match the Average Rate}
\lessonobjective{Apply and interpret the Mean Value Theorem.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
Graph analysis in \emph{The Mean Value Theorem} is a coherent reconstruction problem. Domain, intercepts, limits, derivative signs, critical points, concavity, and asymptotes constrain the same curve. Build the picture in layers rather than trying to sketch from the original formula at once.

Keep a feature table. Each row should state the calculation, the interval or point, and the graphical consequence. This makes the final sketch a summary of evidence instead of an artistic guess.
\end{bgexposition}

\BGVTwoBMVT




\begin{bgexposition}[title={Some instantaneous rate matches the overall average rate}]
The Mean Value Theorem compares the secant line across an interval with tangent lines inside it. For a continuous function that is differentiable inside, at least one tangent has exactly the same slope as the endpoint secant.

In motion language, if a trip averages 60 miles per hour, then at some instant the instantaneous velocity was 60 miles per hour, assuming the position function is smooth enough. The theorem does not identify the instant; it guarantees existence.
\end{bgexposition}

The Mean Value Theorem connects average behavior over an interval with instantaneous behavior at some interior point. If a trip averages \(60\) miles per hour, then under the theorem's smoothness assumptions the instantaneous velocity must equal \(60\) at least once.

This result is far more than a traffic story. It is the engine behind proofs that derivative sign controls monotonicity, that a zero derivative forces a function to be constant, and that derivative bounds control approximation error.

\begin{bgtheorem}[title={Mean Value Theorem}]
If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) and differentiable on \((a,b)\), then there exists at least one \(c\in(a,b)\) such that
\[
\boxed{f'(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}}.
\]
\end{bgtheorem}

The secant slope over the whole interval is achieved by at least one tangent slope inside the interval.

\begin{bgguided}[title={Find the Mean Value Theorem point}]
For \(f(x)=x^2\) on \([1,4]\), find all values \(c\) guaranteed by the theorem.
\begin{bgsolution}
The hypotheses hold because \(x^2\) is a polynomial. The average rate is
\[
\frac{f(4)-f(1)}{4-1}=\frac{16-1}{3}=5.
\]
Since \(f'(x)=2x\), solve
\[
2c=5.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{c=\frac52}.
\]
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexample}[title={A speed interpretation}]
If a car travels \(180\) miles in \(3\) hours and its position is differentiable, then at some instant its velocity is exactly \(60\) mph. The theorem does not identify when, only that such an instant exists.
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgproofidea}
Subtract the secant line from \(f\). The resulting function has equal endpoint values, so Rolle's Theorem gives an interior point where its derivative is zero. That equation is exactly the Mean Value Theorem conclusion.
\end{bgproofidea}


\begin{bgapplication}[title={What an average-speed record guarantees}]
A vehicle travels \(180\) miles in \(3\) hours, with continuous position and differentiable motion during the trip. Its average velocity is \(60\) mph. The Mean Value Theorem guarantees at least one instant when the velocity was exactly \(60\) mph. It does not say when, how many times, or whether the speed ever exceeded \(60\).
\end{bgapplication}

\begin{bgadvanced}[title={The hidden workhorse of elementary analysis}]
The Mean Value Theorem proves much of what introductory calculus casually uses. If \(f'=0\) on an interval, then \(f\) is constant there. If \(f'=g'\), then \(f-g\) is constant. If \(|f'|\le M\), then
\[
|f(b)-f(a)|\le M|b-a|.
\]
These consequences convert local derivative bounds into global control of a function.
\end{bgadvanced}

\section{How the Slopes Themselves Change}
\lessonobjective{Determine concavity intervals and identify genuine inflection points.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
In \emph{Concavity and Inflection Points}, derivatives become evidence about shape. A zero or undefined derivative creates a candidate, a sign chart determines rising and falling behavior, and the second derivative describes how slopes change. No single fact tells the entire graph story.

State intervals, not just isolated points. Explain why a sign has the consequence you claim. When a theorem is used, verify its hypotheses explicitly; continuity and differentiability are not ceremonial phrases but the conditions that make the conclusion reliable.
\end{bgexposition}

\BGVTwoBConcavity




\begin{bgexposition}[title={Concavity asks whether tangent slopes are increasing or decreasing}]
A concave-up graph has slopes that become more positive as \(x\) increases; its tangent lines lie locally below the curve. A concave-down graph has slopes that decrease; its tangent lines lie locally above the curve.

The sign of \(f''\) encodes this behavior. An inflection point requires a change in concavity, not merely a zero of \(f''\). The sign chart must confirm the change.
\end{bgexposition}

Concavity describes how tangent slopes change. If slopes increase as you move right, the graph is concave up; if slopes decrease, it is concave down. The second derivative detects this behavior because it measures the rate of change of the first derivative.

An inflection point requires a change in concavity, not merely \(f''=0\). The zero identifies a candidate. The surrounding sign pattern provides the verdict.

A graph is concave up where \(f'\) is increasing, usually where \(f''>0\). It is concave down where \(f'\) is decreasing, usually where \(f''<0\).

An inflection point is a point on the graph where concavity changes. The condition \(f''(c)=0\) or undefined merely identifies candidates.

\begin{bgguided}[title={Concavity of a quartic}]
For
\[
f(x)=x^4-4x^3,
\]
find concavity intervals and inflection points.
\begin{bgsolution}
\[
f'(x)=4x^3-12x^2,
\]
\[
f''(x)=12x^2-24x=12x(x-2).
\]
Candidate inputs are \(0\) and \(2\). Test signs:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{c|ccc}
interval&\(( -\infty,0)\)&\((0,2)\)&\((2,\infty)\)\\\hline
sign of \(f''\)&+&-&+
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Thus \(f\) is concave up on \(( -\infty,0)\cup(2,\infty)\) and concave down on \((0,2)\). Concavity changes at both candidates. The inflection points are
\[
(0,f(0))=(0,0),
\]
\[
(2,f(2))=(2,-16).
\]
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgmistake}
An inflection point is a point, not only an \(x\)-value. It must belong to the graph. A vertical asymptote may separate concavity intervals but cannot itself be an inflection point because the function is not defined there.
\end{bgmistake}


\begin{bgapplication}[title={Diminishing returns in a learning curve}]
For
\[
M(t)=100-80e^{-0.3t},
\]
we have
\[
M'(t)=24e^{-0.3t}>0,
\qquad
M''(t)=-7.2e^{-0.3t}<0.
\]
The mastery score increases but is concave down: improvement continues while the rate of improvement decreases. Concavity distinguishes ``still getting better'' from ``getting better faster.''
\end{bgapplication}

\begin{bgadvanced}[title={Convexity is a global inequality}]
For a differentiable convex function, every tangent line lies below the graph:
\[
f(y)\ge f(x)+f'(x)(y-x).
\]
When \(f''\ge0\), this inequality can often be proved using the Mean Value Theorem. Convexity matters because any local minimum of a convex function is automatically global, a principle central to optimization and machine learning.
\end{bgadvanced}

\section{Classify Stationary Points with \(f''\)}
\lessonobjective{Apply the Second Derivative Test and recognize inconclusive cases.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
The theorem in \emph{The Second Derivative Test} connects global information on an interval with local derivative behavior inside it. Read the hypotheses and conclusion separately. The theorem guarantees existence of at least one point; it may not identify the point, make it unique, or place it at the midpoint.

Use a diagram to understand the claim, then return to algebra to find candidate values when the problem asks for them. A correct theorem citation should name the interval and explain why each hypothesis is satisfied.
\end{bgexposition}




\begin{bgexposition}[title={The second derivative classifies a horizontal tangent by local bending}]
At a critical point where \(f'=0\), positive \(f''\) means the graph bends upward like a bowl, producing a local minimum. Negative \(f''\) means it bends downward, producing a local maximum.

If \(f''=0\) or does not exist, the test is inconclusive rather than false. Return to the first-derivative test or compare nearby values.
\end{bgexposition}

At a stationary point, \(f''\) measures whether the graph bends upward or downward. Positive second derivative suggests a local bowl and therefore a local minimum; negative second derivative suggests a cap and a local maximum.

When \(f''=0\), the test is inconclusive, not evidence of ``no extremum.'' The first derivative test or direct analysis must take over.

\begin{bgtheorem}[title={Second Derivative Test}]
Suppose \(f'(c)=0\).
\begin{itemize}
\item If \(f''(c)>0\), \(f\) has a local minimum at \(c\).
\item If \(f''(c)<0\), \(f\) has a local maximum at \(c\).
\item If \(f''(c)=0\), the test is inconclusive.
\end{itemize}
\end{bgtheorem}

\begin{bgguided}[title={Classify two critical points}]
For
\[
f(x)=x^3-3x,
\]
classify the critical points.
\begin{bgsolution}
\[
f'(x)=3x^2-3=0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad x=\pm1.
\]
\[
f''(x)=6x.
\]
At \(x=-1\), \(f''(-1)=-6<0\), so there is a local maximum. At \(x=1\), \(f''(1)=6>0\), so there is a local minimum.
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexample}[title={Inconclusive does not mean no extremum}]
For \(f(x)=x^4\), \(f'(0)=0\) and \(f''(0)=0\), but \(0\) is a minimum. For \(g(x)=x^3\), the same two derivative values occur, but \(0\) is not an extremum. Use the First Derivative Test or another argument when \(f''(c)=0\).
\end{bgexample}
